bullets: and explain why you admire them

part2.model: I'd like to talk about my aunt, Farida, whom I've admired for as long as I can remember. She is in her late forties and runs a small bakery in my hometown, which she built up from scratch. A few years ago she was made redundant from a bank, and the whole family assumed she would simply look for another office job. Instead, she took out a modest loan, rented a tiny shop and started baking bread and pastries at four every morning. At first almost nobody came in, and she lost money for months. Even so, she never gave up. Slowly, thanks to word of mouth, the queue began to stretch out of the door, and today she employs six local people. What I admire most is her ability to bounce back from setbacks. I once saw her drop an entire tray of cakes before a big order, yet she just laughed and started again. She is also very down-to-earth, always chatting to customers by name and giving free loaves to elderly neighbours who live alone. I know her because she practically helped raise me, and she taught me to bake my first loaf when I was ten. To me, she leads by example. She showed me that hard work and patience can turn a setback into an opportunity, and that is why I look up to her so much.

vocab.meaning: shows others how to behave by behaving that way herself

questions.q: Why do young people often look up to celebrities rather than ordinary people?
questions.model: I think it mainly comes down to visibility. Celebrities are everywhere on screens, so teenagers feel they know them personally, whereas ordinary heroes rarely make the headlines. There is also a glamorous image that is hard to resist, and it makes success look effortless. However, this can give young people unrealistic expectations. Personally, I'd like the media to shine a spotlight on teachers, nurses and entrepreneurs, because their achievements are far more relatable.

questions.q: Should parents or schools be responsible for providing role models?
questions.model: I think it should be a joint effort. Parents shape a child's values from the very beginning, so their everyday behaviour sets the tone at home. Schools, meanwhile, can help pupils broaden their horizons by inviting inspiring guests, such as local scientists or athletes, to speak to pupils. Ideally the two should work hand in hand. Otherwise, children may pick up their ideas of success from whatever is trending online, which could lead them astray.

questions.q: What might be the drawbacks of having a role model?
questions.model: The main danger is putting someone on a pedestal. If you idolise a person, you may ignore their flaws and be bitterly disappointed when they let you down. Some people also copy a role model's career path exactly, which can stop them from finding their own way. A healthier approach is to take inspiration from certain qualities, such as resilience or generosity, while still learning to think for yourself. That balance keeps admiration healthy.

questions.q: Do you think social media influencers make good role models?
questions.model: Some do, but many don't. The positive ones use their large following to raise awareness of causes or to share practical skills. The problem is that most feeds are carefully curated, so followers see a polished, unrealistic version of life, and that can damage self-esteem. Besides, influencers are often paid to promote products, so their motives are not always sincere. I'd advise young people to take everything online with a pinch of salt.

questions.q: To what extent is success measured by money?
questions.model: To a certain extent, money matters, because financial security gives people freedom and peace of mind. However, I'd argue it is a poor yardstick on its own. Someone can be rolling in money yet feel empty, while a teacher who inspires hundreds of pupils may lead a deeply fulfilling life. In my view, success is about reaching your own goals and having a positive impact on others, rather than chasing a bigger salary.

questions.q: How far do you agree that talent matters more than hard work?
questions.model: I only partly agree. Natural ability gives some people a head start, but it fizzles out without effort. Plenty of gifted students never fulfil their potential because they coast through school, while determined classmates overtake them through sheer persistence. Behind every medal there are years of gruelling training. So, while talent may open the door, it is hard work that keeps you in the room, and I'd say success is mostly perseverance.
